episodes.190829: An approaching upper level low over northern AZ and the Four Corners region overrode abundant low level moisture moving northward into eastern NM. Discrete severe storms developed over portions of northeastern NM during the afternoon with a second area of strong to severe storms located close to the center of the upper level low in northwestern NM. Severe wind gusts and small hail was reported from the discrete storm cells across northeastern NM. These storm cells coalesced and migrated southeastward into the east-central plains of Quay, Curry and Roosevelt Counties by the evening where they produced heavy rainfall that resulted in flash Flooding in Clovis, NM. Earlier, strong wind gusts, accumulating small hail and a landspout were reported with the convection over extremely remote areas of northwestern NM. These storm cells eventually progressed into the Rio Grande Valley where severe winds reached the Albuquerque metro. ||Key Words: Hail, Thunderstorm Wind Gust, Landspout, Flash Flooding.
episodes.190848: A cold front tracking eastward across Montana generated a line of severe thunderstorms   across the eastern half of the state, from late afternoon through the early nighttime hours.  This line eventually moved east into North Dakota.
episodes.190861: A lone severe thunderstorm caused damage in Florence County.
episodes.190924: Isolated storms developed along a weak front that moved through the area. While most of these storms remained below severe limits, one storm did cause tree damage.
episodes.191632: Southwesterly flow aloft allowed for showers and thunderstorms to develop ahead of a quickly advancing cold front June 15 across Central and North-Central Montana. Not many severe-caliber gusts were observed. Additionally, deep mixing across Southwest Montana ahead of the front allowed for a few strong wind gusts there June 15. Along and behind the front, briefly strong non-convective wind gusts were observed along and adjacent to the Rocky Mountain Front.
episodes.191699: Afternoon thunderstorms developed along the Front Range of the Rockies, eventually evolving into an MCS as it pushed east onto the Plains, crossing through the local area during the late evening and overnight hours of Friday the 14th into Saturday the 15th.  As this system passed through, instability was generally in the 1000-2000 j/kg range, but overall deeper layer and effective layer shear values were low, with most of the area less than 30 knots. Thunderstorm activity was widespread across the local area, but no notable hail was reported, and measured winds gusts mainly peaked in the 40-50 MPH range west of Highway 281. The lone exception to these speeds was southeast of Stamford in Harlan County, where a mesonet station measured a gust of 59 MPH shortly before 10:30 PM CDT.
episodes.191700: A building was shifted off its perch as strong winds blew through the Gilead area. The building, consisting of wood posts and aluminum sheeted sides and roof, had a large opening on one end and space near the ground on the sides for airflow. As the gust hit the building, the wind was able to lift the building from the ground up and dislodge/twist it from its original location a small distance. A measured wind gust of 58 mph was recorded near Gilead but winds were likely stronger at the damaged building location.||The damaging thunderstorm was among a small cluster of thunderstorms that formed in north central Kansas and moved northeast along a warm front. The thunderstorms formed at the nose of an axis of 4,000 J/kg CAPE riding into the area aboard 70+ surface dew points.  A clearly defined upper level short wave moved across central Nebraska and triggered the storms, which gained traction initially in an area of 40kt effective shear, though the more favorable shear shifted east fairly quickly, as did the thunderstorms themselves.
episodes.191874: Multiple rounds of training thunderstorms produced an extended period of torrential rainfall across Cheyenne and Morrill counties from the mid to late afternoon into the early evening hours on 6/14. Numerous reports were received of rainfall amounts ranging from 3 to 5 inches in a short period of time, resulting in flash flooding of several county roads due to creeks and streams flowing out of their banks and ditches quickly filling up.
episodes.191930: A few isolated thunderstorms produced quarter size hail and wind gusts around 60 mph.
episodes.192025: Scattered thunderstorms were common across the Billings Forecast Area. Warm temperatures aloft, combined with dry lower levels, resulted in a few of these thunderstorms producing severe wind gusts.
episodes.192225: Thunderstorms developed along a stalled out frontal boundary, which was situated across the middle of Nebraska. As these storms tracked to the southeast, they became severe over southwestern Nebraska. Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 60 MPH were reported along with flash flooding between Lisco and Oshkosh.
episodes.192520: The combined OK/TX Panhandles were hit with a gusty line of storms both on the 13th and 14th of June. Severe winds were the main story with these storms. Ground stations measured wind gusts as high as 80 mph with the storms on the 13th. Then on the 14th, multiple reports of wind damage were made with estimated winds as high as 85 mph, as multiple train cars were knocked over in Cimarron County in OK along with a gain silo damaged in Dallam County in TX.  Then on the 15th Beaver County did see a discrete storm produce some large hail.
episodes.192877: A thunderstorm briefly became severe over eastern portions of Pennington County, producing wind gusts to around 60 mph from Wasta to near Wall.
episodes.192900: On the afternoon of June 14th, a few hours of strong to severe thunderstorms were observed within southeast Ohio. This was the result of a passing cold front tapping into warm surface temperatures, and firing up storms quickly after sunrise across the Ohio Valley. The bulk of the storm damage was observed in the form of downed trees and power lines within southeast Ohio, but an isolated observation of sub-severe hail in Morgan County also occurred. By the evening on the 14th, storms progressed east of the Ohio River into West Virginia, bringing the severe threat in Ohio to an end.
episodes.192908: Daily sea breeze convection under prevailing east wind focused the evening sea breeze collision near the I-75 corridor where locally heavy rainfall and isolated strong storms occurred.
episodes.193314: A line of thunderstorms developed near the Colorado-Kansas border and moved east across Northwest Kansas producing pea to quarter sized hail, and wind gusts estimated to be as strong as 90 mph that produced some damage in Sherman, Sheridan, and Decatur counties. The largest hail fell near the town of Traer in Decatur County. The strongest estimated wind gusts occurred near Norcatur with estimated wind gusts of 90 mph with damage to a garage, chicken coop, and pole barn at a residence.
episodes.193351: Clusters of severe storms moved northeast through the area, producing several areas of wind damage.
episodes.193689: Scattered strong to severe storms produced damaging winds from Hutchinson to Salina during the early afternoon hours of June 15th. Airports in both locations recorded wind gusts up to 77 mph, and widespread damage was reported including downed trees and powerlines as well as a turned over semi truck. Storms also briefly produced large hail up to golf ball size near Hutchinson.
episodes.193741: An upper-level trough of low pressure to the north and west of the Florida Keys assisted in the development of strong convection over the southeast Gulf of Mexico.  Isolated gale-force wind gusts occurred with the stronger thunderstorms from the evening of June 14th through the early morning hours of June 15th, 2024.
episodes.193920: On the morning of the 15th, upper air analysis showed a shortwave trough centered over the High Plains. At the surface, a warm front draped across the Plains slowly lifted north throughout the day, eventually stalling out across eastern Nebraska and down into northwestern Missouri. That afternoon, two areas of thunderstorm development was noted, one in northeast Kansas and another in northeast Nebraska. The thunderstorms in northeast Kansas quickly grew upscale into an MCS bringing strong winds and a brief spin-up tornado to southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa. The thunderstorms in northeast Nebraska were tied to a lingering MCV, with the storm mode initially remaining as clustered supercells. This brought large hail and several tornadoes across northeast Nebraska before finally growing upscale into a second MCS and tracking east into west-central Iowa.

This was a very slow-moving tornado that developed 7 miles south of Meadow Grove, destroying a metal shed and a cattle trailer. Maximum estimated wind speeds in this tornado were 100 miles per hour. The maximum width of this tornado was measured at 300 yards, with an average width estimated at 200 yards.

The office received photo evidence and eyewitness reports of a funnel cloud with a short-lived ground circulation and dust cloud. A brief tornado was determined to have occurred at this location. There were no damage indicators impacted, so the rating of this tornado is EF-U.
Estimated wind gusts.
Water was reported as partially covering county roads near Hoskins to the northeast by emergency management.

A very brief tornado caused window damage to a home and several trees. Maximum winds in this tornado were estimated to be at 84 miles per hour. The width of this tornado was also estimated to be 20 yards.
This is a continuation of the hail swath from Platte County reported to the office from the public. Golf ball sized hail was the largest observed hail size from this event.

Public report of county roads submerged in water. A storm damage survey the next day confirmed several locations where the roads were still under water or partially washed out. By around 7 PM CDT, widespread street flooding was reported in Norfolk. As the storms slowly moved southeast, additional flooding was reported by a county official across central portions of the county where numerous county roads were flooded in addition to considerable lowland flooding.
A funnel cloud was reported by a storm chaser.

Documented from storm chaser video, this tornado developed just northeast of Pilger, north of Highway 275. It then traveled across a feedlot producing minor damage to a sun-shade before crossing into Cuming County. The peak estimated winds in this tornado were 70 miles per hour, with a width of 25 yards.

This is a continuation of the EF-0 tornado that occurred in northeast Stanton County. This tornado did not produce any further damage in Cuming County. The end of the tornadoes track was determined using chaser footage. The peak estimated windspeeds in this tornado were 70 miles per hour, with a width of 25 yards.
